It has been raining for three days, which in this city means that the sidewalks have turned to a slick, dark mirror, and the gutters are singing their low, insistent song. I am standing at the bus stop, not because I need to go anywhere in particular, but because the act of waiting has become a kind of meditation for me, a space where the day's static dissolves into a quieter rhythm. The bus is late, or perhaps it is not late at all; perhaps my watch is the one that is wrong. It does not matter. The rain does not matter. The dampness that has seeped through the soles of my shoes, the way the collar of my coat is slowly drinking the drizzle—these things matter less than the simple physics of the moment: the water falling, the street breathing, and me, here, suspended between one thing and the next.

A woman passes with a yellow umbrella, its fabric so bright it seems to have stolen all the light from the block. She is talking on her phone, her voice sharp and urgent, and I catch a fragment of her sentence: "...but I told them we couldn't wait for the delivery, we have to move forward." Move forward. It is such an American phrase, such a civic religion. We are always moving forward, always optimizing, always treating the present as a lobby for the future. But standing here, with the rain doing its ancient work, I wonder if the idea of moving forward is a kind of fiction, a story we tell ourselves to avoid the uncomfortable truth that most of life is actually just waiting. We wait for the bus. We wait for the email. We wait for the diagnosis, the verdict, the check in the mail. We wait for the weekend, for summer, for the children to grow up, for the mortgage to be paid. We wait for the rain to stop.

And yet, somehow, we pretend we are not waiting.

There is a man a few feet away from me, older, with a gray beard that has a small crumb of something—bread, perhaps, or a pastry—caught in its lower reaches. He is not looking at his phone. He is looking at the sky, or at the awning above the bodega across the street, or at nothing at all. I envy him his vacancy. My own mind is a crowded room, a terminal with too many tabs open. There is the knowledge that I have not written to my sister in three weeks, and that the silence is becoming a thing with its own weight, a stone in the shoe of the relationship. There is the memory of a conversation I had yesterday with a colleague, a conversation in which I said something glib and unkind, and I have been replaying it, trying to find the exact moment where I could have chosen a different word. There is the constant, low-grade hum of the news, the distant thunder of a world that is always on fire. There is the laundry I need to do, the milk that is probably expired, the book on my nightstand that I keep meaning to finish.

The man with the crumb in his beard looks at me, and I look away, embarrassed, as if I have been caught staring. But he does not seem embarrassed. He seems untroubled by the entire category of embarrassment. He is simply there, a figure in a landscape, occupying the space with the same unselfconscious gravity as the lamppost beside him. I think, sometimes, that this is the real goal of a life: not achievement, not happiness, but a kind of full presence, a way of being that does not flinch from the moment. The rain is falling. The bus is not coming. I am here. That should be enough. It never is.

When the bus finally arrives—it is not my bus, it is a different line, a crosstown bus that will take me nowhere useful—I watch the doors hiss open, and a small crowd of people spill out into the rain, their faces set in the expressions of people who have somewhere to be. I let the doors close again. I am not ready to move. Or perhaps I am too ready, too eager to put an end to the waiting, and that eagerness is itself a form of running away. I have been thinking a lot about the idea of patience, about what it means to sit with a feeling without immediately trying to fix it. We are so good at fixing. We are so good at doing. We are terrible at being.

The rain is letting up now, a little. A pale, watery sun attempts a weak appearance, and the streetlights, which have been on all day, begin to look silly, like actors who have forgotten their exit. The man with the crumb has wandered off, and I am alone at the stop, or nearly alone. A young woman has joined me, and she is weeping, quietly, the way people weep in public when they have given up on hiding it. She is not loud. She is not asking for anything. She is just standing there, letting the tears fall, and I realize that I have been so consumed by my own interior drama that I have failed to notice that the world is full of other people who are also waiting, also hurting, also trying to find a way through the day. I want to say something to her. I want to say, "It will be okay," but I don't know that it will be. I want to say, "I understand," but I don't, not really. So I say nothing. I stand there, and we wait together, in the gray light, and there is something almost holy about it, this shared silence, this mutual acknowledgment that the bus is late, and the rain is falling, and we are all just doing our best.

The bus that will actually take me home rounds the corner, its headlights cutting through the mist. I reach into my pocket for my card. The young woman wipes her eyes and steps forward, and we board together, strangers who have shared a moment of the world. I find a seat by the window, and the bus lurches into motion, and the city slides past, smeared with water. I think about the crumb in the man's beard. I think about the yellow umbrella. I think about the young woman, and I hope, weakly, that she is okay. And I think about the word *wait*, how it carries both the sense of time and the sense of service—to wait on someone, to wait tables, to wait for a sign. We are all waiting on something. We are all waiting for the rain to stop. We are all waiting for the moment when the waiting ends.

The bus pulls up to my stop, and I get off. The rain has stopped completely now. The sun is actually out, m hiding behind a bank of silver clouds. The sidewalk is still wet, still a mirror, but now it reflects the sky, and I can see, impossibly, a piece of blue. I stand there for a moment, not moving, not ready to move. And then I walk home, and the door opens, and the day continues, just as it always does, full of waiting and rain and the small, strange grace of being alive.
